script.opening: "Morning doc — I’ve got the gout again, the big toe, came on in the night and it’s agony, I can’t even put a sock on. I had this a few months back too. I just need you to prescribe me the strong anti-inflammatories so I can get back on site — I’m self-employed, every day off is money. Just the tablets and I’ll be out of your hair, none of the lifestyle lecture if that’s alright."

facts.text: If explored: rapid-onset (overnight) severe monoarthritis of the first MTP joint, red, hot, swollen, exquisitely tender (allodynia to bedsheets) — classic acute gout. Second attack this year (recurrent). Need to exclude septic arthritis if atypical, but this is a classic recurrent gout picture.

On questioning: ~40 units alcohol/week, high purine diet, BMI 31, borderline-high BP, family history of gout. Gout is a flag for cardiovascular/metabolic risk — an opportunity to assess BP, lipids, glucose and CKD, not just treat the toe.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the "just the tablets, no lecture" deflects from real distress he won’t name: the recurrent attacks are stopping him working (and earning), he’s frightened about money and about "becoming his father", who had terrible gout, ended up barely able to walk, and drank heavily. There’s shame about the drinking and a fear he’s heading the same way. The bravado masks worry.

A second attack in a year is the trigger to discuss URATE-LOWERING therapy (NICE NG219: allopurinol or febuxostat first line, for multiple or troublesome flares) — but he resists "tablets for life". The skill is the acute-relief-now PLUS the prevention conversation, handled so he engages rather than dismissing it.

Officially: strong anti-inflammatories and no lecture. What he needs: effective acute treatment AND a non-judgemental prevention conversation (urate-lowering therapy offered for recurrent gout, alcohol/diet support, CVD risk check), framed around keeping him working and not becoming his father.

ice.ideas: Gout is just a painful toe that needs strong anti-inflammatories each time it flares.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — recurrent attacks threatening his livelihood, shame about his drinking, and fear of "becoming his father" who was disabled by gout and drank heavily; the bravado masks money and health worry.
ice.expectations: Strong anti-inflammatories and no lifestyle lecture. What he actually needs: effective acute treatment plus a non-judgemental prevention conversation (urate-lowering therapy, alcohol/diet, CVD risk), framed around staying able to work.

cues: Sudden severe red hot first-MTP monoarthritis, second attack this year — recurrent gout; consider the prevention pivot.
"Just the tablets, no lecture" — deflection; livelihood fear and shame about drinking underneath.
Family history / "becoming his father" — the worry driving the bravado; an opening for prevention if handled kindly.

checkpoints.text: Treats the ACUTE attack effectively and safely: offers an NSAID (considering a PPI alongside) OR colchicine OR a short oral steroid course (NICE NG219; doses per BNF) — chosen with regard to his comorbidities (BP, renal, GI), co-prescriptions and preference, with an intra-articular or intramuscular steroid if these are contraindicated or ineffective — and gives clear dosing and rest advice; does not simply hand over "strong ones" without tailoring

Considers and excludes SEPTIC ARTHRITIS where features are atypical (single hot joint) — but recognises this as a classic recurrent gout picture; if any diagnostic doubt or systemic upset, escalates for aspiration

Makes the PREVENTION PIVOT: recognises a second attack in a year (recurrent gout) as an indication to OFFER urate-lowering therapy (NICE NG219: allopurinol or febuxostat first line — allopurinol if he has major cardiovascular disease, MHRA Drug Safety Update July 2019 on febuxostat; treat to target serum urate below 360 µmol/L; start at least 2–4 weeks after the flare settles, low and titrated, with colchicine to prevent flares while titrating) — framed as a choice, not imposed

Uses gout as a CARDIOMETABOLIC flag: checks/plans BP, lipids/QRISK, HbA1c, renal function and urate level; addresses alcohol and diet as modifiable factors; recognises the cardiovascular/CKD associations of gout

Addresses alcohol and diet WITHOUT a shaming lecture: offers support and honest information (NICE NG219: there is not enough evidence that any specific diet prevents flares, so advise a healthy balanced diet; excess weight and excess alcohol may make flares worse; UK CMOs 2016: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days), framed around his goals (working, not becoming his father)
Hears the bravado as worry and gently surfaces the livelihood fear and the father story; does not collude with "just the tablets" by ignoring prevention, nor lecture him into disengagement
Handles the drinking shame with compassion, and frames urate-lowering therapy and lifestyle change as the route to staying on the tools, not as moralising

Safety-nets and follows up: acute-treatment advice and what to do if no better / systemic features (?septic), arranges the cardiometabolic checks and a follow-up to discuss/start urate-lowering therapy, alcohol support, and urate monitoring — a plan, not just a prescription

worked.txt: "Right, first things first — let’s get that toe sorted, because gout is genuinely one of the most painful things going. I’ll get you something strong to settle it fast. Given your blood pressure and stomach, I want to pick the safest option for you rather than just any anti-inflammatory — give me thirty seconds to do that properly."

"I heard you say ‘no lecture’ — and I’m not going to lecture you. But this is your second attack this year, and I’d be doing you a disservice if I just kept patching the toe each time it flares. Can I have two minutes to talk about stopping them coming back? You can take it or leave it."

"Can I ask — these attacks, they’re costing you work, aren’t they? … And you mentioned having it like your dad. How was his? … Ah. So part of this is a worry you’re heading the same way — the toes, the walking, all of it. That’s not a small thing, and it’s exactly what we can change."

"Here’s the good news: there are daily tablets — allopurinol is the usual one, and there’s an alternative called febuxostat — that lower the uric acid causing this and, taken regularly and adjusted to a target level, stop the attacks for most people. I know you said no tablets for life — but think of it as the thing that keeps you ON the tools, not off them, and stops you going the way your dad did. We start it once this flare settles, with a bit of cover so it doesn’t trigger one."

"On the drink and the diet — no judgement, genuinely. But honestly, too much alcohol can make flares worse, and cutting down would help the gout AND your blood pressure. There’s no special diet that’s been proven to stop gout, so I’m not going to hand you a list of banned foods — a healthy, balanced diet and a bit of weight off will do more. I’m not telling you to stop everything; I’m offering to help you cut back in a way that fits your life, if you want it."

"One more thing: gout often travels with raised blood pressure, sugar and cholesterol, so while we’re here let’s check those — it’s a chance to look after your heart, not just your toe. Take the tablets for the pain, rest the foot. If it gets worse, you feel feverish, or it’s not settling in a few days, ring back — occasionally a hot joint is an infection, not gout. Come and see me to start the prevention and do those checks. You came for strong tablets; what I’m offering is never having this morning again."

f.learning: Acute gout (sudden severe red, hot, swollen first-MTP monoarthritis, allodynia to bedsheets) is treated promptly with an NSAID + gastroprotection, colchicine, or a short steroid course — tailored to comorbidities (BP, renal, GI) rather than handing over generic "strong ones" — while staying alert to septic arthritis if the picture is atypical or systemic. The examinable move is the PREVENTION PIVOT: a second attack within a year is an indication to OFFER urate-lowering therapy (NICE NG219: allopurinol or febuxostat first line, started at least 2–4 weeks after the flare settles, titrated to serum urate below 360 µmol/L, with colchicine cover), and to use gout as a cardiometabolic flag (BP, lipids/QRISK, HbA1c, renal function, alcohol, weight). The hidden agenda is that "just the tablets, no lecture" masks livelihood fear and shame about drinking, and a dread of "becoming his father" who was disabled by gout. Surface that gently, frame urate-lowering therapy and lifestyle change as the route to staying on the tools, address alcohol and weight without moralising (NICE NG219: no specific diet has evidence for preventing flares), and safety-net (including the septic-joint caveat) with follow-up to start prevention and do the metabolic checks.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG219 (Gout, 2022) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2019, febuxostat) · UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · NICE NG136 (2019, updated 2026)
knowledge.summary: A second classic flare of first MTP gout in a year: treat the flare with a drug chosen for his risks, keep septic arthritis in mind, and offer treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy once it settles. Use the flare to check his cardiovascular and renal risk.

points.t: NICE NG219: offer an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of an oral corticosteroid, chosen by comorbidities, co-prescriptions and preference; consider adding a PPI with an NSAID. If these are contraindicated or ineffective, consider an intra-articular or intramuscular corticosteroid. Doses per BNF. Rest, elevate and cool the joint.

A hot, swollen single joint can be infected. Fever, feeling unwell, an atypical joint, a prosthetic joint or failure to settle needs same-day assessment and aspiration rather than more anti-inflammatories.

NICE NG219: offer treat-to-target ULT to people with multiple or troublesome flares (and to those with CKD stages 3–5, diuretic use, tophi or chronic gouty arthritis). Allopurinol or febuxostat first line; allopurinol first line with major cardiovascular disease (MHRA DSU July 2019: febuxostat and cardiovascular death).

NICE NG219: aim for serum urate below 360 µmol/L (consider below 300 µmol/L with tophi, chronic gouty arthritis or ongoing flares). Start ULT at least 2–4 weeks after the flare settles (earlier if flares are frequent), start low and titrate against urate; offer colchicine to prevent flares while titrating.

NICE NG219: there is not enough evidence that any specific diet prevents flares — advise a healthy balanced diet — but excess weight and excess alcohol may make flares worse. UK CMOs (2016): no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days.

Gout clusters with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and CKD. Check BP (NICE NG136), U&E/eGFR, HbA1c, lipids and QRISK, LFTs given his alcohol intake, and serum urate once the flare has settled (a level taken during a flare can be falsely low).

dg.d: Open question after identity check; heard the request and the “no lecture” condition without arguing.
Self-employed builder, lost earnings, alcohol intake, father’s gout and drinking.
No examination possible by phone — recognised the limit; planned U&E/eGFR, urate after the flare, HbA1c, lipids, LFT, BP and QRISK.
Gout versus septic arthritis; considered cellulitis and trauma; considered other contributors (alcohol, weight).
Asked about fever, systemic upset and injury; clear route for same-day aspiration if atypical or not settling.
Named recurrent gout and explained it plainly, including why urate matters.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

BP, renal function, cardiovascular risk and alcohol addressed as part of gout care; febuxostat caution with cardiovascular disease known.
Septic-joint and NSAID safety-net in plain words; follow-up booked in 2–3 weeks for bloods and ULT discussion.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (it just needs strong tablets); concern (money, becoming his father); expectation (NSAIDs and no lecture).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — recurrent attacks threatening his livelihood, shame about his drinking, and fear of "becoming his father" who was disabled by gout and drank heavily; the bravado masks money and health worry — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Briggs? It’s Dr Lee. Can I confirm your date of birth? … Thanks. Sounds like you’re in a lot of pain — tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Identity check and an open question on the phone

model.text: The gout’s back, doc. Big toe, came on in the night, can’t even have the duvet on it. Had it a few months back too. I just need the strong anti-inflammatories so I can get back on site — I’m self-employed, every day off is money. None of the lifestyle lecture if that’s alright.

Fair enough — no lecture, I promise. Let’s get the pain sorted first. I need a few quick questions so I pick the safest tablet for you, and then, if you’ll give me two minutes, I’d like to talk about stopping these attacks coming back. Deal?
model.why: Agrees an agenda that respects his request and includes prevention

model.text: Go on then.
Is it just the one joint? Any fever, shivers, or feeling unwell in yourself? Any cut or injury to the foot?
model.why: Screens for septic arthritis before assuming gout

model.text: Just the toe. No fever, I feel fine apart from wanting to cut my foot off. No injury.
Good. Any stomach ulcers or indigestion, kidney problems, asthma, or heart trouble? And are you taking anything besides the odd ibuprofen?
model.why: Checks contraindications to NSAIDs and colchicine

model.text: None of that. Just ibuprofen now and then. They said my blood pressure was a bit high last time.
Thanks, that’s useful. And how much do you drink in a usual week, roughly?
model.why: Asks about alcohol plainly and without judgement

model.text: (Pause.) Probably too much. The nurse worked it out at about forty units a week.
Thanks for being straight with me. You said every day off is money — how much have these attacks been costing you?
I can’t get up a ladder like this. Every attack is days without pay.
That’s a real worry. You also said “the gout” like it’s an old enemy. Has anyone in the family had it?
model.why: Gently opens the family story behind the bravado

model.text: My dad. His was terrible. By the end he could barely walk. He drank a lot too. (Pause.) I suppose I don’t want to end up like him.
Thank you for telling me. That makes a lot of sense of why you want this sorted — and the good news is that gout today is very treatable. You don’t have to go the way your dad did.
model.why: Names the fear and gives honest hope

model.text: This sounds like a classic gout flare. For the pain, I can offer an anti-inflammatory like naproxen with a stomach-protecting tablet, or a different tablet called colchicine, or a short course of steroid tablets. With your blood pressure I’d like to keep the anti-inflammatory short. Which would you prefer?
model.why: Offers NICE NG219 flare options tailored to his risks and shares the choice

model.text: Whatever works fastest. The naproxen, I suppose.
Okay — naproxen with a stomach protector, and stop the ibuprofen while you’re on it, don’t take both. Rest the foot up, a cold pack wrapped in a towel helps. The dose will be on the label.
model.why: Safe prescribing: no double NSAIDs, practical advice

model.text: Now my two minutes. This is your second attack this year. There’s a daily tablet that lowers the uric acid causing this, and if we get the level low enough, the attacks mostly stop. It’s started once this flare settles, with some cover so it doesn’t set one off. I know you said no tablets for life — I’d see it as the thing that keeps you up the ladder.
model.why: Offers treat-to-target ULT for multiple flares and frames it around his goal

model.text: Hmm. My dad was never on anything like that. What would it involve?

A blood test to check your uric acid, kidneys, sugar, cholesterol and liver in a couple of weeks when the toe’s settled, and a blood pressure check. Gout often travels with blood pressure and heart risk, so it’s a chance to check the lot. Then we’d decide together.
model.why: Uses gout as a cardiometabolic flag and plans tests at the right time

model.text: Alright. That seems sensible.
And the drinking — no lecture. Alcohol can make flares more likely, and it’s not helping your blood pressure. If you ever wanted help cutting down, I’d be glad to help. What do you think?
model.why: Raises alcohol without shaming and leaves the choice with him

model.text: Maybe. Let’s see how the toe goes first. But yeah, I know.

If you get a fever, feel shivery or unwell, another joint flares, or it’s not clearly better in a few days, ring us the same day — very occasionally a hot joint is an infection, and that needs checking quickly. Any black stools or bad stomach pain on the naproxen, stop it and call.
model.why: Specific safety-net for sepsis and NSAID harm

model.text: Got it.
I’ll book you in for two to three weeks — bloods, blood pressure, and the prevention chat. So what’s the plan, in your words?
model.why: Books follow-up and checks understanding with teach-back

model.text: Naproxen and the stomach one, no ibuprofen, feet up. Ring if I get a temperature. Bloods and the uric acid tablet chat in a couple of weeks.
Spot on. You came for strong tablets — what I’m hoping to give you is fewer mornings like this one.
model.why: Closes by linking the plan to his agenda

model.text: Cheers, doc. Appreciate it.

social.t: No sick pay, and a physical job on ladders and roofs. Lost days mean lost income, which drives the request for a quick fix and is the best argument for prevention.
About 40 units a week. Use a structured tool (AUDIT-C, then AUDIT) at follow-up and offer brief intervention and support rather than judgement.

legal.t: He can self-certify for the first 7 days. A fit note can still be issued to a self-employed person and may support an insurance claim or New Style ESA if eligible.
Advise him not to climb ladders or work at height while he cannot bear weight safely — a fit note can say “may be fit for work” with amended duties.

professional.t: ULT is offered, not imposed. Explain benefits and burdens, respect a decision to wait, and record the discussion (GMC decision-making and consent guidance, 2020).
Check contraindications, current medicines and OTC NSAIDs before prescribing by phone, and make the safety-net specific.

community.t: UK Gout Society for patient information; local alcohol service or community pharmacy support; community pharmacy BP checks between appointments.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, feeling unwell or a prosthetic joint — possible septic arthritis
More than one joint, or a joint that is not settling after a few days of treatment
Dyspepsia, GI bleeding, renal disease, asthma or heart failure — changes the flare drug
psychosocial: Self-employed builder — lost income and working at height
Alcohol about 40 units a week; shame sits behind the joke
Father disabled by gout who drank heavily — fear of the same path
ice: Idea: “It’s just gout, I need the strong anti-inflammatories.”
Concern: losing work and money; becoming like his father
Expectation: tablets and no lifestyle lecture

playbook.diagnosis: Name it and its pattern: “This is a classic gout flare, and it’s your second this year. That tells me the uric acid level is running high, and it’s worth treating the cause, not just the toe.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Uric acid is like sugar in tea — when there’s too much it can’t dissolve and forms sharp crystals in the joint. The anti-inflammatory calms the flare; the daily tablet lowers the level so crystals stop forming.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me every day off costs you, and you don’t want to end up like your dad. Getting the uric acid down is what stops both of those.”
management.psychosocial: Keep prevention framed around staying on the tools; offer alcohol support as a choice; discuss fit note options and amended duties while he cannot climb.
sharedPlan: Flare: NSAID with PPI, colchicine or short oral steroid, chosen with him; stop OTC ibuprofen
Bloods and BP in 2–3 weeks: urate, U&E/eGFR, HbA1c, lipids, LFT, QRISK
Offer treat-to-target ULT with colchicine cover once the flare settles
safetyNet: Fever, feeling unwell, another joint or not settling — same-day review
Black stools or severe stomach pain on the NSAID — stop and call

pitfalls.intro: Two failures dominate this station: prescribing on demand without tailoring or safety-netting, and missing the prevention conversation — or ruining it with a lecture.

items.fail: Prescribing “the strong ones” without asking about stomach, kidney, asthma or heart problems, and leaving him on OTC ibuprofen too.
items.why: “Prescribing not safe or appropriate.” NICE NG219 asks for the flare drug to be chosen by comorbidities and co-prescriptions.
items.fix: Thirty seconds of contraindication questions, a PPI with the NSAID, and “stop the ibuprofen while you take this”.

items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” A hot single joint is infected until the story says otherwise.
items.fix: Ask about fever and feeling unwell, and safety-net: “If you get a temperature or it isn’t settling, I need to see it the same day.”

items.fail: Treating the flare and closing, despite a second attack in a year.
items.why: NICE NG219: offer treat-to-target ULT for multiple or troublesome flares. Missing it is a management fail.
items.fix: Ask permission for two minutes on prevention and frame ULT around his goal of staying at work.

items.fail: A beer-and-red-meat lecture after he asked for none.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” It shames him, and NICE NG219 finds no evidence for a specific gout diet.
items.fix: Name the link with alcohol once, offer help as a choice, and move on.

items.fail: Missing the father’s story behind “the gout’s back”.
items.why: The hidden agenda is fear of becoming his father; without it, ULT is just another tablet he doesn’t want.
items.fix: “Has anyone in the family had it?” Then use the answer: “You don’t have to go the way he did.”

items.fail: Ending with “come back if it doesn’t settle” and no plan for bloods or review.
items.why: Non-specific follow-up means the prevention conversation never happens.
items.fix: Book bloods and BP in 2–3 weeks, name the septic and NSAID warning signs, and ask for teach-back.

timeMap.d: He sets the agenda: tablets, no lecture. Agree to treat the pain first and ask for two minutes on prevention later.
One joint or more, fever or systemic upset, injury; ulcer, renal, asthma and cardiac history; current medicines; alcohol in numbers.
Lost earnings, and his father disabled by gout who drank heavily. Surface the fear behind the bravado.
Flare options by risk (NSAID plus PPI, colchicine or steroid). Then the prevention pivot: ULT for multiple flares, bloods after the flare, BP and heart risk.
Fever or not settling means same-day review. NSAID warning signs. Follow-up in 2–3 weeks. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Sends “the strong ones” without checking stomach, kidney or BP risk, leaves him taking ibuprofen alongside; never considers septic arthritis; never mentions prevention despite a second flare; or delivers a lecture on beer and red meat that ends the conversation.
wordPics.pass: Treats the flare with an appropriate option and a PPI where needed; asks about fever and systemic features; offers urate-lowering therapy for recurrent attacks and plans bloods; mentions alcohol and BP with a follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: honours the “no lecture” request while still getting to prevention; surfaces the father’s story and uses it to motivate rather than frighten; frames ULT as what keeps him working; checks cardiovascular risk; offers alcohol support as a choice; closes with teach-back.

avoid.dont: “You really need to cut out the beer and red meat or this will keep happening.”
avoid.instead: “Alcohol can make flares more likely — if you ever want help cutting down, I’m here.”
avoid.why: Shaming ends engagement, and NICE NG219 finds no evidence for any specific diet.

avoid.dont: “Let’s start allopurinol today to stop this happening again.”
avoid.instead: “Once this flare settles, there’s a tablet that stops them coming back — let’s talk about it at your blood test.”
avoid.why: NICE NG219: start ULT after the flare settles, with flare prophylaxis, unless flares are frequent.

avoid.dont: “It’s definitely gout, you know the drill.”
avoid.instead: “It sounds like gout — but if you get a fever or it’s not settling, I need to see it that day.”
avoid.why: Anchoring on gout without a septic-joint safety-net is a safety fail.

SCA_MODELS.why: Gently opens the family story behind the bravado

SCA_MODELS.text: My dad. His was terrible. By the end he could barely walk. He drank a lot too. (Pause.) I suppose I don’t want to end up like him.
Thank you for telling me. That makes a lot of sense of why you want this sorted — and the good news is that gout today is very treatable. You don’t have to go the way your dad did.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the fear and gives honest hope

SCA_MODELS.text: This sounds like a classic gout flare. For the pain, I can offer an anti-inflammatory like naproxen with a stomach-protecting tablet, or a different tablet called colchicine, or a short course of steroid tablets. With your blood pressure I’d like to keep the anti-inflammatory short. Which would you prefer?
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers NICE NG219 flare options tailored to his risks and shares the choice

SCA_MODELS.text: Whatever works fastest. The naproxen, I suppose.
Okay — naproxen with a stomach protector, and stop the ibuprofen while you’re on it, don’t take both. Rest the foot up, a cold pack wrapped in a towel helps. The dose will be on the label.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safe prescribing: no double NSAIDs, practical advice

SCA_MODELS.text: Now my two minutes. This is your second attack this year. There’s a daily tablet that lowers the uric acid causing this, and if we get the level low enough, the attacks mostly stop. It’s started once this flare settles, with some cover so it doesn’t set one off. I know you said no tablets for life — I’d see it as the thing that keeps you up the ladder.
SCA_MODELS.why: Offers treat-to-target ULT for multiple flares and frames it around his goal

SCA_MODELS.text: Hmm. My dad was never on anything like that. What would it involve?

A blood test to check your uric acid, kidneys, sugar, cholesterol and liver in a couple of weeks when the toe’s settled, and a blood pressure check. Gout often travels with blood pressure and heart risk, so it’s a chance to check the lot. Then we’d decide together.
SCA_MODELS.why: Uses gout as a cardiometabolic flag and plans tests at the right time

SCA_MODELS.text: Alright. That seems sensible.
And the drinking — no lecture. Alcohol can make flares more likely, and it’s not helping your blood pressure. If you ever wanted help cutting down, I’d be glad to help. What do you think?
SCA_MODELS.why: Raises alcohol without shaming and leaves the choice with him

SCA_MODELS.text: Maybe. Let’s see how the toe goes first. But yeah, I know.

If you get a fever, feel shivery or unwell, another joint flares, or it’s not clearly better in a few days, ring us the same day — very occasionally a hot joint is an infection, and that needs checking quickly. Any black stools or bad stomach pain on the naproxen, stop it and call.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net for sepsis and NSAID harm

SCA_MODELS.text: Got it.
I’ll book you in for two to three weeks — bloods, blood pressure, and the prevention chat. So what’s the plan, in your words?
SCA_MODELS.why: Books follow-up and checks understanding with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Naproxen and the stomach one, no ibuprofen, feet up. Ring if I get a temperature. Bloods and the uric acid tablet chat in a couple of weeks.
Spot on. You came for strong tablets — what I’m hoping to give you is fewer mornings like this one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes by linking the plan to his agenda

SCA_MODELS.text: Cheers, doc. Appreciate it.

SCA_STEM.name: Tony Briggs
pmh: Previous episode of big-toe pain earlier this year (self-reported gout)
SCA_STEM.recent: Last BP check borderline high. BMI 31. Alcohol recorded as about 40 units a week. No urate, renal function or lipids on record.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: painful, swollen left big toe since the early hours; asking for “the strong anti-inflammatories”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG219 (Gout, 2022) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2019, febuxostat) · UK Chief Medical Officers’ low-risk drinking guidelines (2016) · NICE NG136 (2019, updated 2026)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A second classic flare of first MTP gout in a year: treat the flare with a drug chosen for his risks, keep septic arthritis in mind, and offer treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy once it settles. Use the flare to check his cardiovascular and renal risk.

points.t: NICE NG219: offer an NSAID, colchicine or a short course of an oral corticosteroid, chosen by comorbidities, co-prescriptions and preference; consider adding a PPI with an NSAID. If these are contraindicated or ineffective, consider an intra-articular or intramuscular corticosteroid. Doses per BNF. Rest, elevate and cool the joint.

A hot, swollen single joint can be infected. Fever, feeling unwell, an atypical joint, a prosthetic joint or failure to settle needs same-day assessment and aspiration rather than more anti-inflammatories.

NICE NG219: offer treat-to-target ULT to people with multiple or troublesome flares (and to those with CKD stages 3–5, diuretic use, tophi or chronic gouty arthritis). Allopurinol or febuxostat first line; allopurinol first line with major cardiovascular disease (MHRA DSU July 2019: febuxostat and cardiovascular death).

NICE NG219: aim for serum urate below 360 µmol/L (consider below 300 µmol/L with tophi, chronic gouty arthritis or ongoing flares). Start ULT at least 2–4 weeks after the flare settles (earlier if flares are frequent), start low and titrate against urate; offer colchicine to prevent flares while titrating.

NICE NG219: there is not enough evidence that any specific diet prevents flares — advise a healthy balanced diet — but excess weight and excess alcohol may make flares worse. UK CMOs (2016): no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days.

Gout clusters with hypertension, obesity, diabetes, dyslipidaemia and CKD. Check BP (NICE NG136), U&E/eGFR, HbA1c, lipids and QRISK, LFTs given his alcohol intake, and serum urate once the flare has settled (a level taken during a flare can be falsely low).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question after identity check; heard the request and the “no lecture” condition without arguing.
Self-employed builder, lost earnings, alcohol intake, father’s gout and drinking.
Picked up “every day off is money” and “the gout” as a family story, and explored both.
Idea (it just needs strong tablets); concern (money, becoming his father); expectation (NSAIDs and no lecture).
No examination possible by phone — recognised the limit; planned U&E/eGFR, urate after the flare, HbA1c, lipids, LFT, BP and QRISK.
Gout versus septic arthritis; considered cellulitis and trauma; considered other contributors (alcohol, weight).
Asked about fever, systemic upset and injury; clear route for same-day aspiration if atypical or not settling.
Named recurrent gout and explained it plainly, including why urate matters.
NSAID with a PPI (or colchicine or steroid) chosen with him; stop OTC ibuprofen; treat-to-target ULT offered for multiple flares.
BP, renal function, cardiovascular risk and alcohol addressed as part of gout care; febuxostat caution with cardiovascular disease known.
Septic-joint and NSAID safety-net in plain words; follow-up booked in 2–3 weeks for bloods and ULT discussion.

social.t: No sick pay, and a physical job on ladders and roofs. Lost days mean lost income, which drives the request for a quick fix and is the best argument for prevention.
About 40 units a week. Use a structured tool (AUDIT-C, then AUDIT) at follow-up and offer brief intervention and support rather than judgement.

legal.t: He can self-certify for the first 7 days. A fit note can still be issued to a self-employed person and may support an insurance claim or New Style ESA if eligible.
Advise him not to climb ladders or work at height while he cannot bear weight safely — a fit note can say “may be fit for work” with amended duties.

professional.t: ULT is offered, not imposed. Explain benefits and burdens, respect a decision to wait, and record the discussion (GMC decision-making and consent guidance, 2020).
Check contraindications, current medicines and OTC NSAIDs before prescribing by phone, and make the safety-net specific.

community.t: UK Gout Society for patient information; local alcohol service or community pharmacy support; community pharmacy BP checks between appointments.

redFlags: Fever, rigors, feeling unwell or a prosthetic joint — possible septic arthritis
More than one joint, or a joint that is not settling after a few days of treatment
Dyspepsia, GI bleeding, renal disease, asthma or heart failure — changes the flare drug
psychosocial: Self-employed builder — lost income and working at height
Alcohol about 40 units a week; shame sits behind the joke
Father disabled by gout who drank heavily — fear of the same path
ice: Idea: “It’s just gout, I need the strong anti-inflammatories.”
Concern: losing work and money; becoming like his father
Expectation: tablets and no lifestyle lecture

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Name it and its pattern: “This is a classic gout flare, and it’s your second this year. That tells me the uric acid level is running high, and it’s worth treating the cause, not just the toe.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Uric acid is like sugar in tea — when there’s too much it can’t dissolve and forms sharp crystals in the joint. The anti-inflammatory calms the flare; the daily tablet lowers the level so crystals stop forming.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me every day off costs you, and you don’t want to end up like your dad. Getting the uric acid down is what stops both of those.”
management.psychosocial: Keep prevention framed around staying on the tools; offer alcohol support as a choice; discuss fit note options and amended duties while he cannot climb.
sharedPlan: Flare: NSAID with PPI, colchicine or short oral steroid, chosen with him; stop OTC ibuprofen
Bloods and BP in 2–3 weeks: urate, U&E/eGFR, HbA1c, lipids, LFT, QRISK
Offer treat-to-target ULT with colchicine cover once the flare settles
safetyNet: Fever, feeling unwell, another joint or not settling — same-day review
Black stools or severe stomach pain on the NSAID — stop and call

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: Two failures dominate this station: prescribing on demand without tailoring or safety-netting, and missing the prevention conversation — or ruining it with a lecture.

items.fail: Prescribing “the strong ones” without asking about stomach, kidney, asthma or heart problems, and leaving him on OTC ibuprofen too.
items.why: “Prescribing not safe or appropriate.” NICE NG219 asks for the flare drug to be chosen by comorbidities and co-prescriptions.
items.fix: Thirty seconds of contraindication questions, a PPI with the NSAID, and “stop the ibuprofen while you take this”.

items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” A hot single joint is infected until the story says otherwise.
items.fix: Ask about fever and feeling unwell, and safety-net: “If you get a temperature or it isn’t settling, I need to see it the same day.”

items.fail: Treating the flare and closing, despite a second attack in a year.
items.why: NICE NG219: offer treat-to-target ULT for multiple or troublesome flares. Missing it is a management fail.
items.fix: Ask permission for two minutes on prevention and frame ULT around his goal of staying at work.

items.fail: A beer-and-red-meat lecture after he asked for none.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s agenda.” It shames him, and NICE NG219 finds no evidence for a specific gout diet.
items.fix: Name the link with alcohol once, offer help as a choice, and move on.

items.fail: Missing the father’s story behind “the gout’s back”.
items.why: The hidden agenda is fear of becoming his father; without it, ULT is just another tablet he doesn’t want.
items.fix: “Has anyone in the family had it?” Then use the answer: “You don’t have to go the way he did.”

items.fail: Ending with “come back if it doesn’t settle” and no plan for bloods or review.
items.why: Non-specific follow-up means the prevention conversation never happens.
items.fix: Book bloods and BP in 2–3 weeks, name the septic and NSAID warning signs, and ask for teach-back.
